nameStory: The 'spined' part of this spider's name comes from the dramatic spiky projections jutting out from its abdomen, making it look like a tiny medieval fortress. The alternative name 'castleback orbweaver' captures this armored appearance perfectly, as if someone built battlements on a spider's back.
description: The Spined Micrathena is a small but unmistakable orbweaver spider that looks like it's wearing medieval armor. These tiny architects spin moderately large, tightly coiled webs that can stretch about 8 inches across. The spiders themselves are quite small, ranging from about 4 to 11 millimeters long, but their spiky abdomens make them impossible to miss. Their venom is completely harmless to humans, making them safe garden neighbors.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The abdomen has distinctive sharp spines or spikes jutting out from the sides and back, feeling hard and rigid like tiny thorns if gently touched

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Black and white patterned body with some individuals showing bright yellow patches along the sides of the abdomen

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates a tightly coiled orb web up to 8 inches across with very precise, closely-spaced spiral threads that feel sticky to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider body measuring less than half an inch long, though the spines make it appear larger and more intimidating

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active during daylight hours and rarely seen at night, typically sitting in the center of their web waiting for prey

habitat: Found in wooded areas, forest edges, and gardens throughout New England where they can string their webs between shrubs, tree branches, and tall plants. They prefer spots with some protection from wind but enough open space to build their substantial webs. Look for them in areas with mixed vegetation at heights ranging from knee-high to just above head level.

seasonality.spring: Young spiders are developing but rarely seen, as they haven't yet reached their distinctive spiky adult form.
seasonality.summer: Adults begin appearing and building webs, but they're most easily spotted later in the season when fully mature.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity period when these spiders are most visible and active in their webs, displaying their full spiky armor.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off after laying eggs, which overwinter and hatch the following year.

funFact: Despite looking like a fearsome medieval weapon, the Spined Micrathena's spikes are actually a defense mechanism against birds - the spines make the spider too awkward and potentially painful for birds to swallow, essentially turning the spider into a living caltrop.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the Arrow-shaped Orbweaver, but the Spined Micrathena has multiple spikes all around its abdomen while the Arrow-shaped has just two prominent rear spikes. Memory trick: Spined = Spine-y all around, Arrow-shaped = points backward like an arrowhead.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name 'Micrathena' means 'small Athena,' referencing the Greek goddess of wisdom and warfare - quite fitting for these small but well-armored spiders that demonstrate remarkable engineering skills in their web construction.
compareHints: Unlike its cousin the Arrow-shaped Orbweaver which has two prominent rear spikes, the Spined Micrathena bristles with multiple spines around its entire abdomen. The White Micrathena lacks the dramatic yellow coloring and has a more uniformly white and black pattern. The Spined Micrathena's spikes are also more numerous and create a more 'porcupine-like' appearance compared to its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Micrathena relatives in New England, the Arrow-shaped is the only one with a truly triangular, arrow-like abdomen.
Compared to its relatives in the Micrathena genus, the White Micrathena is distinguished by its glossy black coloration with contrasting white markings and golden-brown legs.
